Conviction of Sin
kuhn-VIK-shun of SIN
n. phrase
From Latin convincere, to overcome, prove guilty; the sense rendering the Greek elenchō, to reprove or convince, in Christ's promise that the Comforter would "reprove the world of sin" (John 16:8).

📖 Biblical Definition

Conviction of Sin is the work of the Holy Ghost whereby He so applies the law and the gospel to a man's conscience that he is brought to see, feel, and own his guilt before a holy God. The Lord Jesus promised this ministry: "And when he is come, he will reprove the world of sin, and of righteousness, and of judgment" (John 16:8). The verb is elenchō, to convict as a court convicts the guilty—not merely to inform of sin in the abstract, but to fasten guilt upon the conscience so that the sinner cannot evade the verdict. This conviction has both a preparatory and an ongoing aspect. Preparatory, it is that work by which the Spirit, often through the preached law, slays the sinner's self-righteousness, stops his mouth, and shows him guilty before God (Rom 3:19), so that, despairing of himself, he flees to Christ. Such was Peter's congregation at Pentecost, who, hearing the word, were "pricked in their heart, and said... Men and brethren, what shall we do?" (Acts 2:37). Ongoing, conviction continues in the believer, the Spirit using the word to humble him under remaining sin, to keep him tender of conscience, and to drive him afresh to the blood of Christ for cleansing. It is therefore the Spirit's instrument against all easy-believism, which would have men profess faith without ever feeling the weight of their sin or the need of a Savior. A gospel that never convicts has never converted. Yet conviction is not its own end and must not be confused with saving faith; it is the Spirit's plough breaking up the fallow ground, that the seed of the gospel may take root, and it always aims beyond itself at Christ. This dictionary confesses conviction of sin as a true and necessary work of the Spirit, humbling the sinner and the saint alike, and ever driving the convicted soul not to despair but to the cross.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines CONVICTION as the act of convincing of sin; the state of being convinced or convicted by conscience; the act of compelling one to admit the truth. Conviction of Sin is the Spirit's reproving work fastening guilt upon the conscience (John 16:8).

expand to see more

CONVICTION, n. — 1. The act of convincing, or compelling one to admit the truth of a charge. 2. In law, the act of finding a person guilty. 3. The act of convincing of sin, or the state of being convinced; the state of the conscience under a sense of guilt.

In the spiritual sense, Conviction of Sin is the Holy Ghost's work of reproving the conscience so that the sinner sees, feels, and owns his guilt before God.

"And when he is come, he will reprove the world of sin, and of righteousness, and of judgment" (John 16:8).

It requires the Spirit to slay self-righteousness and drive the sinner to Christ; it forbids the easy-believism that professes faith without any sense of sin.

It is the plough breaking the fallow ground, never an end in itself, but always aiming beyond itself at the cross of Christ.

📖 Key Scripture

John 16:8 — "And when he is come, he will reprove the world of sin, and of righteousness, and of judgment."

Acts 2:37 — "Now when they heard this, they were pricked in their heart, and said unto Peter and to the rest of the apostles, Men and brethren, what shall we do?"

Romans 3:19 — "Now we know that what things soever the law saith, it saith to them who are under the law: that every mouth may be stopped, and all the world may become guilty before God."

Psalms 51:3 — "For I acknowledge my transgressions: and my sin is ever before me."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Conviction of Sin is corrupted by the easy-believism that omits it altogether, offering a decision without any sense of guilt, and by the morbid scrupulosity that stops at conviction and never moves on to Christ.

expand to see more

The dominant corruption of our age is easy-believism, which strips conviction of sin out of the gospel altogether. Sinners are urged to make a decision, say a prayer, or accept Christ without ever being brought to feel the weight of their guilt or the justice of their condemnation; sin is minimized, the law is muted, and the wrath of God against the sinner is left unmentioned for fear of giving offence. But the Spirit's appointed order is to reprove the world of sin (John 16:8), and the apostolic preaching pierced the heart and provoked the cry, "what shall we do?" (Acts 2:37). A faith that was never preceded by any sense of need has nothing to lay hold of in a Savior, for they that be whole need not a physician. The recovery of the doctrine requires the recovery of law-preaching: that men may know their guilt, despair of themselves, and so be driven to Christ. False peace is the great danger of an unconvicted profession.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The opposite error, less common but real, is to make conviction an end in itself—a morbid, introspective dwelling on guilt that never rises to faith in Christ. Some souls, truly awakened, sink under the burden of sin and stay there, treating the depth of their sorrow as if it were a qualification for grace, when conviction is meant only to empty the hand that it may receive Christ. The positive biblical principle to recover is that conviction always aims beyond itself: it is the Spirit's plough, not His harvest; it breaks the ground that the gospel seed may take root. Therefore the convicted soul is to be pointed at once away from his sin and his sorrow alike, and toward the cross, where the blood of Christ cleanseth from all sin—for godly sorrow worketh repentance unto salvation, not to be repented of.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

The doctrine rests on Christ's promise that the Comforter would elenchō (reprove, convict) the world of sin (John 16:8), fastening guilt upon the conscience that the sinner may flee to Christ.

expand to see more

Greek elenchō (G1651) — to convict, reprove, expose; the verb of John 16:8, the Spirit convicting the world of sin.

Hebrew yakach (H3198) — to reprove, correct, decide; the Old Testament background of the Spirit's reproving work.

Greek katanyssō (G2660) — to prick sharply, pierce; the verb of Acts 2:37, the hearers pricked in heart.

Greek lype (G3077) — sorrow, grief; the godly sorrow that worketh repentance unto salvation (2 Cor 7:10).

Conviction is the Spirit's plough, preparatory and ongoing, ever aiming beyond itself at the cross of Christ.

Usage

"Under the preaching of the law, deep Conviction of Sin laid hold of him, and he cried out, like Peter's hearers, "what shall I do?""

"Easy-believism dispenses with Conviction of Sin, offering a Savior to those who have never felt themselves lost."

"Conviction of Sin is the Spirit's plough, not His harvest—it breaks the heart only that the gospel seed may take root in Christ."
